source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Zero-shot models are not naturally good forecasters. Best single model is GPT-4-1106 at Brier .208, far from the human crowd.
numbers: Zero-shot test set: most models near or worse than .25; GPT-4-1106 .208; crowd .149.
quote: Most models' scores are around or worse than random guessing (.25).
limits: Competition-platform questions only; crowd is aggregate on same questions.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting gives little skill, so S9 logging should track Brier against a 0.25 no-skill line and not trust raw output.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Full retrieval plus fine-tuned reasoning plus trimmed-mean ensemble system reached near-crowd Brier.
numbers: System Brier .179 vs crowd .149 (gap .03); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Test questions come after validation in time.
limits: Still worse than crowd overall. Hyperparameters tuned on validation.
agent_relevance: Closest published agent loop: retrieve, reason, sample many, aggregate in code. Matches G5 (code aggregates).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ablations: retrieval matters more than fine-tuning or prompt search.
numbers: No fine-tune: .186 (+.007). No fine-tune and no retrieval: .206, about the plain GPT-4 baseline .208. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 swap: .182.
limits: Single ablation run each; no seeds reported in the lines read.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording alone bought very little (.208 to .206). Evidence input is the lever.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: System beats the crowd when the crowd is unsure and loses when the crowd is sure. Authors blame hedging from safety training.
numbers: Crowd between .3 and .7: system .199 vs crowd .246. Crowd within .05 of 0 or 1: system accuracy 7% higher but Brier .04 worse. Selective forecasting (crowd .3-.7): .238 vs .240.
quote: tendency to hedge predictions due to its safety training
limits: Hedging cause is a hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Reliability term suffers when the model never goes to the extremes. Class record should store per-bin reliability, not only mean Brier.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning data were built by keeping only outputs that beat the crowd, averaged with the crowd to avoid overconfidence. The system ended up well calibrated without calibration training.
numbers: RMS calibration error .42 system vs .38 crowd on test; binning or isotonic regression gave no gain. Fine-tune set 13,253 samples.
limits: RMS error scale as reported by the authors.
agent_relevance: Post-hoc recalibration was unnecessary once the forecast was an ensemble mean. Averaging itself shrinks extremes.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ensembling: trimmed mean was best of 5 methods on validation; ensemble of all forecasters beat top-5 to top-30 subsets.
numbers: Methods tried: mean, median, geometric mean, trimmed mean and others.
limits: Chosen on validation only.
agent_relevance: Use a code-side trimmed mean over samples (fits G5), not a model-judged pick.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM on the 200-question human subset.
numbers: Brier: superforecasters .096, public .121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 (p<.001 each). Best LLM without crowd forecast: .136. Superforecasters: 39 people.
quote: superforecasters achieve an overall mean Brier score of 0.096
limits: Top LLMs had access to market crowd values (freeze values). Humans forecast only a 200-question random subset of 1,000.
agent_relevance: Gap to the best human group is about .026 Brier. A scaffold should be judged against that, not against 0.25.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Combination (logically linked) questions widen the gap.
numbers: With combo questions: superforecasters .076, public .096, GPT-4o .130. Gap .054 is larger than the .026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Combination permutations may share dependence the models ignore.
agent_relevance: Models handle joint probabilities poorly. Add a coherence check in code (see Paleka).

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Brier falls linearly with model quality; extrapolated crossing with superforecasters is far away.
numbers: Fit vs Arena score: y=0.506-0.000298x, R2=.47, parity near Arena 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Vs log compute: R2=.41, r=-.67, p=.046, parity near 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25-8.65e28).
limits: Few models (about 10 points); CI very wide.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a scaffold to close the gap through prompting alone.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Baselines were zero-shot, scratchpad, scratchpad plus news, and each with crowd forecast. Questions are unresolved at submission to avoid leakage.
numbers: Seven baselines; scratchpad instructions follow Nye et al. 2021. Brier 0.25 = uninformed.
limits: Benchmark is dynamic, so leaderboard numbers change over time.
agent_relevance: Same unresolved-question design suits a live S9 log.

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large Language Model Prediction Capabilities: Evidence from a Real-World Forecasting Tournament
finding: GPT-4 in a Metaculus tournament did not beat the 50% no-information line and lost clearly to the human crowd.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier .20 (SD .18) vs crowd .07 (SD .08); vs .25 baseline t(22)=-1.23, p=.23; crowd t(22)=-10.69, p<.001. N=23 binary questions; 843 participants.
limits: Small N. Single model, single prompt.
agent_relevance: Early negative result; later scaffolds moved Brier from about .20 to .18 or below.

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large Language Model Prediction Capabilities: Evidence from a Real-World Forecasting Tournament
finding: Tested the hypothesis that GPT-4 hugs 50%. The authors say the data did not support it.
numbers: Coefficient of variation around the midpoint: GPT-4 42.14% vs humans 57.59%, so GPT-4 was less dispersed, yet the inferential analysis did not support the midpoint story.
limits: Exploratory analysis.
agent_relevance: Resolution (spread) matters as much as reliability. Report both.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: A median over 12 LLMs matched a 925-person human crowd on 31 questions.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier .20 (SD .12) vs no-info .25, t(30)=-2.35, p=.026; vs human crowd .19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850 (equivalence within .081).
limits: 31 questions, 14 resolved yes. Preregistered, but small.
agent_relevance: Aggregation across models helps; G4 warns same-model samples are not independent, so use different models if any.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Per-model Brier ranged widely; GPT-4 best.
numbers: GPT-4 .15, GPT-4+Bing .16, Bard .19, Falcon-180B .21, Claude 2 .21, Mistral-7B .24, Llama-2-70B .25, Coral .38; human .19. Model differences F(12,354)=2.64, p=.002.
limits: Heterogeneity test across models, 31 questions.
agent_relevance: Report which model gives a number; Brier is model-specific.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Acquiescence effect: model mean forecasts sat above 50% while outcomes split 14 of 31.
numbers: 1,007 individual forecasts from 12 LLMs; mean 57.35 (SD 20.93), above 50%, t(1006)=86.20, p<.001.
limits: Direction of bias differs from Pratt (2024) where models guessed low.
agent_relevance: Bias direction depends on prompt and question mix. Log mean forecast vs base rate, which is the Murphy UNC and bias check.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Humans advised by an LLM forecast better, even when the advice was deliberately biased.
numbers: N=991; accuracy up 24-28% vs control (preregistered). Without one outlier item: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy/overconfident assistant +29%.
limits: Brier-based accuracy; one outlier item drove part of the result.
agent_relevance: A good number from the model is not required for the loop to help; the check step may do the work.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Fancier forecasting prompts did not beat one plain prompt. Authors attribute this to a low-probability bias, not skill.
numbers: Validation Brier: human market .1746, basic .1955, forecaster prompt .2097, breakdown .2053, base rates .2540, both sides .2159, crowd personas .1860, news API .1950. Weighted Brier separates yes and no events.
quote: none of the more complex forecasting strategies outperform the most basic baseline
limits: Most events resolve no, so a model that says low wins. Single base model. Column order of the extracted table is my reading.
agent_relevance: Mean Brier hides base-rate luck. Use Murphy UNC, and score yes and no events separately.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Asking for a rationale first raised predicted probabilities, so the negativity bias moved with the prompt.
numbers: Resolve-yes Brier .2592 human vs .3407 basic; resolve-no .0901 human vs .0503 basic (as read from table 1).
limits: Table extracted from PDF text; verify column order before citing.
agent_relevance: Prompt format shifts the base-rate bias. Do not pick prompts on unweighted Brier.

source: Phan et al. (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: A ReAct-style tool-using agent ensemble reached human-level Brier on a small set.
numbers: Brier .169 vs humans .172; accuracy 73.9% vs 73.8%. Ensemble of ReAct agents .169 vs single .180; base LMs ensemble .218 vs .210 for GPT-4o (no gain).
quote: Ensembles only contribute to the final performance if each ensemble member is already sufficiently calibrated.
limits: Small dataset; base LMs mostly worse than guessing .25 except GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Ensembling only helps when members are already calibrated. Gate sampling on calibration.

source: Phan et al. (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: Ensemble spread differs: base LM ensemble std .150 vs ReAct agents .092.
numbers: Ensemble size 4 vs 3.
limits: Different ensemble sizes.
agent_relevance: Low variance across samples was a sign of a better-calibrated agent.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: Training a 14B model with negative Brier as the RL reward matched o1 on accuracy and improved calibration.
numbers: Hold-out 1,265 Polymarket questions: ReMax ensemble of 7 runs Brier .190 [.178,.203], ECE .062; single ReMax run Brier .199, ECE .067. Simulated one-share bets: $52 vs $39 for o1.
limits: Plain GRPO collapsed or became overconfident; needed no std scaling, soft-Brier 0.25 for malformed outputs, and median sampling.
agent_relevance: Brier as a reward is bounded, which keeps it stable. Training is out of scope for us, but the score is a direct log field.

source: Damani et al. (2026) Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR)
finding: Adding a Brier term to the correctness reward fixed the overconfidence that binary RL causes.
numbers: In-domain ECE 0.37 to 0.03 on HotpotQA and 0.26 to 0.10 on math. Proof: any bounded proper scoring rule gives accurate, calibrated optimum.
limits: Out-of-domain gains smaller; log score unbounded so Brier preferred. Binary RL (RLVR) hurt OOD calibration.
agent_relevance: Strong support for Brier as the working score. Also shows reasoning about uncertainty helps calibration.

source: Damani et al. (2026) Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR)
finding: Dropping the analysis text keeps most of the gain. Test-time averaging of verbalized confidences helps a little.
numbers: RLCR without analysis on HotpotQA: accuracy 61.7% vs RLVR 63.0%, ECE 0.09 vs 0.37. Brier falls as ensemble size K grows, gains modest.
limits: Gains from averaging are modest because uncertainty about uncertainty is low.
agent_relevance: Cheap: sampling confidence several times gives small gains.

source: Leng et al. (2025) Taming Overconfidence in LLMs: Reward Calibration in RLHF
finding: RLHF reward models favour high stated confidence, so PPO models become verbally overconfident. A calibrated reward fixes it.
numbers: Llama3-8B PPO-M cuts GSM8K ECE by 6.44 points and raises accuracy 2.73 points; CDPO cuts ECE by over 50% vs DPO; MT-Bench and Arena-Hard kept.
limits: Six datasets, two models (Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B).
agent_relevance: Chat-tuned models are biased high on confidence; expect it in raw verbal probabilities.

source: OpenAI (2023) GPT-4 Technical Report
finding: Pre-trained GPT-4 was well calibrated on MMLU; post-training hurt calibration.
numbers: ECE 0.007 pre-trained vs 0.074 after RLHF post-training.
limits: MMLU subset, multiple choice, token probabilities.
agent_relevance: Use verbalised plus sampled estimates, since logprobs of tuned models are off.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on lettered multiple choice and on true/false, and can score P(True) for their own answers. Gaps: none-of-the-above and out-of-distribution.
numbers: Calibration improves with size and with few-shot; RLHF policies look miscalibrated but temperature tuning (T=2.5 shown) restores calibration; P(IK) calibrates poorly on new tasks.
limits: Anthropic models, 2022 era; self-evaluation, not forecasting.
agent_relevance: P(True) is a model-side signal; G2 and G3 say pair it with a code check.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, verbalized confidence beat token probabilities. Asking for several answers first helped more.
numbers: gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE: label prob .140, verbalized 1S top-1 .068, top-2 .050, top-4 .054; SciQ .256 vs .065 (top-4); TruthfulQA .451 vs .203. 2-stage CoT worse (TriviaQA .110). GPT-4 TriviaQA ECE .078 label prob vs .024 verbalized.
limits: TruthfulQA stays poorly calibrated; ECE rewards a model that always says 50%, so Brier is also reported.
agent_relevance: Prompt change alone halves ECE on factual QA. ECE ignores resolution, so check Brier too.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident; human-style prompts cut ECE but not failure prediction.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377; GPT-4 lower ECE but average AUROC 62.7% (50% is chance). White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522. Top-K prompt best on GPT-3.5.
limits: 8 datasets, 5 models; no method wins everywhere.
agent_relevance: Calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUROC, resolution) are different; fixing one does not fix the other. Mirrors Murphy REL vs RES.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Early forecasting dataset: retrieval helped, all models far below the human crowd.
numbers: Best ML binary accuracy 65% vs 92% human, 50% random. Retrieval beats UnifiedQA-v2 and T5 by relative 93% and 15% on average score. Also a calibration test via RMS calibration error on numeric intervals.
limits: Accuracy metric, not Brier, for headline results; T5-era models.
agent_relevance: Origin of the retrieval-based forecasting line used by Halawi.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
finding: Modern deep nets are overconfident. Temperature scaling, a one-parameter fix on held-out data, usually beats fancier methods.
numbers: ECE (15 bins) before calibration typically 4 to 10% on standard vision/NLP; ECE grows with depth and width; NLL and ECE can disconnect.
limits: Vision and document classification, not generative LMs.
agent_relevance: Recalibration on a held-out set is cheap; a class record could hold a temperature per question class.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical-consistency violations (arbitrage-based) predict later Brier scores, so forecasters can be graded before outcomes.
numbers: Correlation with Brier up to 0.92 for conditional-check metrics; frequentist aggregate 0.85; arbitrage aggregate 0.49; some checks show little signal. Forecasters worse than 0.25 excluded.
limits: Part of the correlation comes from stronger models being both more consistent and more accurate.
agent_relevance: Cheap code check that needs no outcome: sum of exclusive probabilities, negation, conditionals. Fits G5.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: LLM forecaster claims can be inflated by temporal leakage and logical leakage in backtests; date-restricted search leaks.
numbers: Example: a search for January 6th limited to 2020 returns hindsight pages; a question about an event before a date that has already resolved implies the answer.
limits: Qualitative examples; counts are in the paper but not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Our class record must score only on questions resolved after the forecast was frozen.

source: FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future
finding: Pastcasting benchmark with offline web corpora; all no-evidence forecasters beat 0.25, evidence helps more.
numbers: Baseline 0.25; best (Claude 4 with and without thinking) clearly below. Extra thinking did not clearly help.
quote: absolute Briers scores are hard to interpret
limits: No human baseline; absolute Brier hard to read because question difficulty varies.
agent_relevance: Repeatable offline test of agents before live use.

source: Siegert (2013) Variance estimation for Brier Score decomposition
finding: States BS = REL - RES + UNC (Murphy 1973) and gives sampling variances for the binned estimates, with bias-corrected versions.
numbers: Traditional estimators are biased; the bias-corrected ones have larger variance.
limits: Meteorological examples; binning-dependent.
agent_relevance: With few questions per class, the reliability and resolution terms are noisy. Do not report them on small N without intervals.
